conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I’ll be helping manage your care today. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, doctor. Honestly, I’m in a lot of pain—more than usual. It’s that same crampy, colicky feeling, but worse on the right side. I threw up about two liters of greenish fluid last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned this has been going on for a while, but this episode was worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I usually vomit a few times a day, but not this much. And my G-tube isn’t helping like it used to. They switched me to a smaller, more flexible one, and it just doesn’t drain well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ve reviewed your CT scan from this morning. It shows that the loops of your small bowel are more dilated than before—about 5 to 6 centimeters—which suggests your chronic partial bowel obstruction may be a bit worse right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So it’s not a new blockage, just the old one acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s the same area, likely in the left lower quadrant, just a little more distended. Surgery was consulted, and they agree no operation is needed at this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had enough surgeries. What’s the plan then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now to let your bowel rest. You’ll get IV fluids, and we’ll restart your TPN through your femoral line once we’re sure things are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And for pain? I know my usual ER protocol is up to 1 mg of IV Dilaudid over an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s still the plan. We’ll start with 0.25 mg every 15 minutes as needed, up to 1 mg total. We’ll also give you Phenergan for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I usually don’t take narcotics at home, so I don’t want to get used to them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. This is just for acute flare-ups like today. We’ll use it short-term and then stop once you’re back to baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’ve had a dose of Dilaudid and Phenergan. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still there, but not as sharp. The nausea’s calmed down too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your labs came back—white count is normal, no signs of infection. Your kidney and liver function are stable. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a headache earlier. I use butorphanol nasal spray at home, but I didn’t bring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you a dose of Fioricet, and the nurse said your headache improved quickly. We can arrange for butorphanol to be sent from home or pharmacy if you’d like.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’d be great. It works better for me than anything else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been watching you for a few hours. Your pain is more manageable, and you haven’t vomited since admission. We’re going to try a small sip of water to see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I haven’t had anything to drink in hours. I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You kept the water down, so we’re advancing to clear liquids. If you do well, we may try soft food tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What about my G-tube? I really think it’s not working as well since the change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. The team agrees it may not be decompressing effectively. You’re scheduled to follow up with your GI doctor to discuss switching back to a larger tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That’s been bothering me a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did really well overnight—no vomiting, pain is down, and you tolerated a soft diet. Your repeat labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So does that mean I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re going to discharge you today. We’ll restart your TPN at home, and you can resume all your regular medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No changes to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: None. Everything stays the same—your gabapentin, clonidine, octreotide, all of it. We’ll send a list with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Dilaudid protocol for future ER visits?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s still valid. The ER and your pain team know the plan: up to 1 mg IV Dilaudid over an hour, with Phenergan if needed, then discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’d like to avoid being admitted again if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We agree. This stay was just to get you through a flare-up safely. Your condition is stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the fatty liver the CT mentioned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s been seen before and is stable. It’s likely related to your TPN. Your hepatology team monitors that, and no new action is needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my iron and thyroid meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue both. Your anemia is chronic, and thyroid levels are stable. Keep taking levothyroxine and ferrous sulfate daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my femoral line? It’s clean, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, site is clean and dry. Keep using the ethanol lock as prescribed after TPN to prevent infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. A nurse will go over discharge instructions, and you should follow up with your GI doctor about the G-tube. Feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you only if you really need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly with your discharge paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Just keep monitoring your symptoms and reach out if things worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.
